“you know, lost souls are not that different from those in the zone. the zone is enjoyable, but when that joy becomes an obsession, one becomes disconnected from life.” you have to admit to dissect the nature of the afterlife and telling it through an older, childless, single, black man is awesome… but to tell a story about a dead black man who lives in black communities in america, reaching the pearly gates of the great beyond, and then doing all that while not mentioning jesus once is some backbreaking gymnastics that it’s almost impressive. and, despite that, it still feels like they kept their cards too close to their chest. it still feels like spirituality and heaven by committee. how do we include the least religion possible here? how do we make the movie about dying but keep our tail so far between our legs that you can’t see it? make every dead person on the travelator an old person who is ready to die, that rings true doesn’t it? how do we make the movie about jazz in black communities, have almost exactly half of it, and then ignore the rest of those spaces? how do we cover our arse by saying the great before and beyond is a hypothetical place, even though we’ve seen and made a more interesting cultural depiction of death before in ‘coco’? there also some funny nitpicks i have, things you only really realise once you think too hard. let me just go for the throat, there’s no point in wasting time: if this movie declares that people have personalities before they’re born, does this movie inadvertently say that life begins at conception? what are you doing? why would you put yourself in a position? i don’t hate this movie! if you watch it you’re gonna get a visually arresting and a beautifully animated film here, with specific touches like accuracy on musical instrument performance, some nice film grain, diversity, and mood lighting that will absolutely knock your socks off. ‘soul’ is a very impressive and slick piece of visual production. this movie is about adulthood careers as opposed to childhood dreaming which cuts to the heart of something honestly quite mature. this movie might not be the highlight of your week, but it would be a night well spent.

Feels like one of those Pixar films that displays so much potential in the first 20 minutes in setting up some poignant message about grappling with our own sense of mortality, and Reznor and Ross' soundtrack accompanied with Jon Batiste is a worthy companion. But the movie stumbles over its own footing as it gets lost trying to narrow down and convey what exactly the underlying message of its story is. Is finding your "spark" supposed to be about realizing that your lifelong passion isn't actually lucrative and you should find something more sustainable if you can't make a living off it? Or is it about coming to terms with the idea that your lifelong ambition isn't always what it turns out to be and it's okay to just start anew? Or that your life still has purpose even if you feel like you haven't fulfilled what it is you thought you were meant to do? It becomes so convuluted by the end and these questions still go unanswered, so the emotional baggage you're left with doesn't feel nearly wrapped up as well as it could've been. Ultimately comes off as a visually and sonically captivating Pixar installment (still thought the "Great Beyond" looked and sounded cool af) but with a lot of unfulfilled potential in its central storyline and main character arc — coupled with an antagonist that's honestly not very memorable either. I liked it enough to stay entertained on my flight, but given the overall content and musical appreciation prevalent throughout its runtime, I do wish I ended up loving it more.

One of the most visually stunning Pixar movies that they've ever made, but when you watch it, it kind of begs the question: who is this for? In the 90s, Disney went chasing Oscars with Pocahontas and Hunchback of Notre Dame, and made movies that were too silly for adults and too serious for kids, so they ended up being mostly for nobody. Although Soul is a superior film to those two examples, this movie certainly has the same vibe. Soul has a lot of talk about Jazz theory and the astral plane, so it has a lot of stuff that's going to go over kids' heads; but it also has a talking cat and a lot of pratfalls, so it feels too unserious for adults. It's a movie about a sad middle-aged guy who dies but gets stuck in an ethereal plane and has to learn about the beauty of a mundane existence. But, you know, for kids. The movie is beautiful to look at and has an amazing score. This is one of those movies where a guy has to prove that he's amazing at playing an instrument and the times that he plays ACTUALLY sounds amazing. But ultimately that movie has a crazy mishmash of different tones. One of the climaxes of this movie involves calming down a little anxiety demon who keeps repeating, "I'm not good enough," which is something Pete Docter does again in Inside Out 2, only better.
Although I had to cry and love the theme/topic and characters and the music. I cried harder watching Coco and that sits at 4 stars. So naturally there has to be a bit of a gap between these.

Fuckass movie In all honesty, I've been going through a rough path for a couple of months now and I’ve been feeling a lot like 22 at the beginning of the movie. Everything about life is just « meh », I’ve slowly been loosing passion for my hobbies and passions, just kinda stopped caring overall about everything, becoming more cynical by the minute. I was just thinking about what I wanted to do in the future and how once I get to that point I’ll be fine and life will finally be great. When Joe stands on the sidewalk after the performance - the one he always wanted, the one that would change everything - he simply appears normal, or rather empty. His life isn’t changed like he always said it would be. It’s still pretty much the same overall, even if he achieved his dream. He achieved his « purpose », so what’s next? As he plays the piano all by himself in his dark apartment, he remembers the joyful moments of his life and yes music and jazz is there, but that’s not all there is. It’s the mundane things of everyday life. I also really liked the story of his barber friend, how he wanted to be veterinarian but bc he needed money for his daughter hospital bills, he took up barber lessons and he’s now the best there is. Becoming a barber wasn’t in his plans, as he said so himself, but he’s still happy being one bc isn’t that the whole point anyway? The message of the movie isn’t anything revolutionary per say, it isn’t the first time I’ve heard it, but I did need to hear it once again lately. Life is all about the small moments between the big events, that’s when you are truly living. My big events will come, but that doesn’t mean I have to sit here and do nothing in the mean time, I can live a little.

Très bien, et vraiment beau. Joe Gardner est professeur de musique à New York et ne vit que pour le jazz. Le jour où il décroche enfin le concert de sa vie, il tombe dans une bouche d'égout et se retrouve dans l'au-delà. Il refuse d'y aller, et se retrouve associé à une âme qui, elle, refuse de naître. Ce qui rend le film remarquable, c'est son sujet. Pixar demande si une vie qui ne réalise pas sa vocation est une vie ratée, et répond non. Le film déplace la question de la passion vers celle de ce qui nous anime vraiment au quotidien, et c'est un propos rare pour un film familial. Docter matérialise des concepts abstraits avec une aisance hallucinante. Le Grand Avant, le Grand Bazar, l'océan des âmes égarées, et ces entités en charge de l'au-delà représentées par de simples traits en mouvement. On reproduit l'exploit de Vice-versa. La musique fait énormément, et le film a deux univers sonores : le jazz de Jon Batiste pour la Terre, ce sont ses mains qu'on voit jouer, rotoscopées  et les nappes éthérées de Trent Reznor et Atticus Ross pour le monde des âmes. Ma réserve : il y a quelques égarements scénaristiques au milieu, notamment le long passage dans un corps de chat. Premier Pixar avec un héros de couleur. Oscars du film d'animation et de la musique.

Fakat filmin sonuna doğru, aslında ona ne kadar benzer hissettiğimi fark ettim. Hayatta hep bir amacımız olması gerektiği düşüncesi, gerek üzerimizdeki baskılar gerekse içinde büyüdüğümüz kültür tarafından sürekli önümüze konuyor. Film bunlara “spark” demiş. Fakat bu spark’ın illa ki hayatımızın amacı olması gerektiğini düşünmek, bence çok yanlış bir kalıplaşmış düşünce. Bunu bu filmi izledikten sonra asıl fark ettim. C’est ça qui est touchant et puissant, puis en termes d’images, grâce au génie des productions de l’ampleur de disney, ça permet de sublimer certains arts, comme en ce cas précis la musique (en plus sur des genres et cultures qui sont très importantes en termes d’histoire et de culture : le jazz, la soul…).
